confirmed: The source is the 26-page arXiv 2510.23904v2 dated 31 Jan 2026, formatted for CHI 2026 with DOI 10.1145/3772318.3790375; title and author list match (PDF p. 1 and document page count). The entire markdown, including Appendices A-D, was read.

Randomized within-person condition order is explicit, with equal distribution across sequences; every participant used both MultiColleagues and ChatGPT on the same self-chosen problem (PDF p. 8, Section 4.2). This is a randomized people study for the two-screener pipeline.

lab_rct is consistent with researcher-supervised sessions conducted remotely via Zoom; participants were recruited through university mailing lists and professional networks rather than an online panel (PDF p. 7, Sections 4.1-4.2).

The sample comprises 20 people: 15 students and 5 early-career professionals, aged 20-39, with 9 males and 11 females (PDF p. 7, Section 4.1 and Table 2). Both conditions involve the same participants; paired t(19) analyses support 20 analyzed people, and no post-assignment exclusions are reported (PDF pp. 8 and 12, Sections 4.2 and 5.3.1).

Both conditions used GPT-4o; this is an ai_design comparison without a no-AI condition. Ideation was planned for approximately 10 minutes per condition, with flexible stopping, within approximately 70-minute sessions (PDF pp. 7-8, Section 4.2).
Originality statistics match exactly: MultiColleagues M = 3.78, SD = 0.38; Baseline M = 3.59, SD = 0.44; W = 70.0, p = .202 (PDF p. 13, Section 5.3.3).

The originality method uses GPT-5, full conversations, a 5-point rubric, and three independent runs averaged per idea set; human-rater validation was not performed (PDF pp. 12-13, Section 5.3.3; p. 18, Section 6.6; p. 23, Appendix B.2).

Topic branching is sub-topics divided by main topics, using GPT-5 topic segmentation, three runs averaged, and two researchers checking topics with Cohen's kappa = 0.86 (PDF p. 9, Section 4.3.3). Its reported values match: MultiColleagues M = 6.45, SD = 2.54; Baseline M = 3.50, SD = 1.79; t(19) = 5.15, p < .001 (PDF p. 12, Section 5.3.1; p. 13, Figure 5).
The concept-production numbers embedded in S1-O2 are correct: 2.05 concepts/min, SD = 0.81 versus 1.26, SD = 0.67; t(19) = 2.59, p < .05 (PDF p. 12, Section 5.3.1; p. 13, Figure 5).

Perceived Quality & Novelty is self-report from Q5 and Q7 on 7-point scales. Values match: MultiColleagues 5.95 +/- 0.92; Baseline 4.97 +/- 1.16; W = 17.0, p < .01, r = 0.69 (PDF p. 12, Table 6 and Section 5.3.3; p. 22, Appendix A.2). It does not itself satisfy the output-scoring criterion.

Criteria 1 and 3 are met through random condition order and scored originality/contributions; criterion 2 fails because only 20 people were analyzed. core = no and context_class = none are correct for this small randomized experiment (PDF pp. 7-9, Sections 4.1-4.3.3; pp. 12-13, Sections 5.3.1 and 5.3.3; creativity-codebook.md, Sections 3-4).

Topic branching concerns each participant's contributions; Table 4 linguistic scores concern participants' own text, not similarities between different people. No across-people homogenization estimate is reported (PDF p. 9, Section 4.3.3; p. 11, Table 4; p. 22, Appendix B.1).

This is an original empirical study, not a synthesis; no pooled estimates or synthesis study counts need extraction (PDF pp. 7-13, Sections 4-5). Appendices A-D contain questionnaires, scoring/topic-extraction prompts, and system details rather than additional comparative creativity estimates (PDF pp. 21-26).
summary: A randomized within-person study of 20 analyzed people belongs in the two-screener pipeline but falls below the core sample-size threshold. Reported numbers and source version match; a separate concept-production outcome, missing outcome metadata and statistics flags, and the nonsignificance wording need correction.
